TORT LIABILITY FOR HIRING A COMPETITOR’S AT-WILL EMPLOYEES (REEVES V. HANLON; BUXBOM V. SMITH; DELLA PENNA; KOREA SUPPLY; IXCHEL PHARMA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, summarizes what California law says about the tort exposure of an employer that hires, or solicits, employees who work for a competitor under employment terminable at will. It is organized around the California Supreme Court’s decision in Reeves v. Hanlon (2004) 33 Cal.4th 1140, which held that a plaintiff suing over interference with an at-will employment relation must plead and prove an independently wrongful act, and around the authorities Reeves drew on and the authority that later extended it: Buxbom v. Smith (1944) 23 Cal.2d 535, Della Penna v. Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A., Inc. (1995) 11 Cal.4th 376, Korea Supply Co. v. Lockheed Martin Corp. (2003) 29 Cal.4th 1134, and Ixchel Pharma, LLC v. Biogen, Inc. (2020) 9 Cal.5th 1130. It also sets out the text of Business and Professions Code section 16600, the statute Reeves cited for the state’s policy favoring employee mobility. Where a specific hiring employer and a specific competitor are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Borealis Systems, LLC; the sheet can equally be read on its own, with no party named, as a general reference. It describes what the cited authorities say and hold. It does not evaluate any particular hire, solicitation, resignation, or departure, does not state whether any conduct was or was not independently wrongful, and does not predict how any court would rule.

THE STANDARD REEVES V. HANLON ADOPTED FOR INTERFERENCE WITH AN AT-WILL EMPLOYMENT RELATION
Reeves v. Hanlon arose from the departure of two attorneys from a Los Angeles immigration firm and their recruitment of the firm’s staff to the new firm they formed. The California Supreme Court took the case to decide whether a defendant may be held liable on an intentional interference theory for having induced an at-will employee to quit working for the plaintiff. The court answered that such a claim is governed not by the rules for interference with an existing contract but by the standard applicable to claims for intentional interference with prospective economic advantage, because an interference with an at-will relation is primarily an interference with the future relation between the parties. The operative requirement, stated twice in the opinion — once in the introduction and again in the discussion — is that the plaintiff plead and prove an independently wrongful act that induced the at-will employee to leave. The court described the standard as serving two policies at once: guarding against unlawful methods of competition in the job market, and protecting both the right of at-will employees to pursue opportunities for economic betterment and the right of employers to compete for talented workers. The court stated in the same passage that the standard makes clear that solicitation or hiring alone is not an actionable wrong.

WHAT REEVES SAYS ABOUT OFFERING A COMPETITOR’S EMPLOYEE MORE PAY OR BETTER TERMS
Having adopted the independent-wrongfulness standard, the Reeves court stated the corollary expressly: a defendant is not subject to liability for intentional interference where the interference consists merely of extending a job offer that induces an employee to end at-will employment. The court placed that corollary in a policy frame drawn from the earlier cases it had surveyed, observing that where no unlawful methods are used, public policy generally supports a competitor’s right to offer more pay or better terms to another’s employee so long as the employee is free to leave, and quoting Judge Learned Hand’s observation in Triangle Film Corp. v. Artcraft Pictures Corp. that a contrary rule would be intolerable to employers who could use the employee more effectively and to employees who might receive added pay, and would put an end to any kind of competition. The opinion does not identify a category of solicitation that is wrongful in itself; under the standard it announced, the wrongfulness must come from an act proscribed by some independent legal standard.

THE ELEMENTS OF INTENTIONAL INTERFERENCE WITH CONTRACTUAL RELATIONS AS REEVES STATES THEM
Before turning to at-will relations, Reeves restated the settled elements of the older tort of intentional interference with contractual relations, drawing them from Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. Bear Stearns & Co. (1990) 50 Cal.3d 1118. The court listed five: a valid contract between the plaintiff and a third party; the defendant’s knowledge of that contract; the defendant’s intentional acts designed to induce a breach or disruption of the contractual relationship; actual breach or disruption; and resulting damage. On the intent element, Reeves added, citing Quelimane Co. v. Stewart Title Guaranty Co. (1998) 19 Cal.4th 26, 56, that the plaintiff need not prove the defendant acted with the primary purpose of disrupting the contract but must show the defendant’s knowledge that the interference was certain or substantially certain to occur as a result of the defendant’s action. These elements do not include independent wrongfulness; that is the point on which the at-will line of cases turns.

THE PROSPECTIVE-ADVANTAGE TORT: ITS ELEMENTS, AND WHAT "INDEPENDENTLY WRONGFUL" MEANS (KOREA SUPPLY)
Because Reeves routed at-will employment claims to the prospective-advantage standard, the elements of that tort govern. Korea Supply Co. v. Lockheed Martin Corp. traced those elements to Buckaloo v. Johnson (1975) 14 Cal.3d 815, 827, and set out the customary five-part formulation: an economic relationship between the plaintiff and some third party carrying the probability of future economic benefit to the plaintiff; the defendant’s knowledge of the relationship; intentional acts by the defendant designed to disrupt it; actual disruption; and economic harm proximately caused by the defendant’s acts. Korea Supply also held that the tort carries no requirement of specific intent to disrupt: it is enough to plead that the defendant knew the interference was certain or substantially certain to occur as a result of its action. Reeves restated the same five elements in its own footnote 6, citing Youst v. Longo (1987) 43 Cal.3d 64, 71, footnote 6. Korea Supply also supplied the definition that Reeves imported into the at-will employment setting. The court held that an act is independently wrongful if it is unlawful — that is, if it is proscribed by some constitutional, statutory, regulatory, common law, or other determinable legal standard. The opinion paired that definition with a limit: an act is not independently wrongful merely because the defendant acted with an improper motive, and the tort is not intended to punish individuals or commercial entities for their choice of commercial relationships or their pursuit of commercial objectives unless their interference amounts to independently actionable conduct. In the case before it, the court found the requirement satisfied by allegations that the defendant’s agent had violated the federal Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Reeves quotes the same definition verbatim when it states the at-will employment standard.

WHERE THE INDEPENDENT-WRONGFULNESS REQUIREMENT CAME FROM (DELLA PENNA V. TOYOTA)
The independent-wrongfulness requirement entered California law in Della Penna v. Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A., Inc., which held that a plaintiff suing for interference with prospective contractual or economic relations must plead and prove, as part of its case-in-chief, that the defendant not only knowingly interfered with the plaintiff’s expectancy but engaged in conduct wrongful by some legal measure other than the fact of interference itself. The court grounded the rule in a distinction between a formed contract and an expectancy: a damage remedy is provided against third party conduct intended to disrupt an existing contract because the exchange of promises resulting in such a formally cemented economic relationship is deemed worthy of protection from a stranger to the agreement, whereas economic relationships short of contractual stand on a different legal footing so far as tort liability is reckoned. The opinion added that because the culture is wedded to the social rewards of commercial contests, the law usually takes care to draw lines of legal liability in a way that maximizes areas of competition free of legal penalties. Reeves quoted the first of those passages when it explained why an at-will relation resembles an expectancy more than a cemented contract.

THE OLDER RULE: BUXBOM V. SMITH ON HIRING ANOTHER’S EMPLOYEES AND LOSING THE IMMUNITY
Sixty years before Reeves, the California Supreme Court in Buxbom v. Smith addressed a defendant who had induced the plaintiff to build up a distribution crew to serve a contract, then repudiated the contract and hired the crew. The opinion states the general rule that competitive means such as advertising or price-cutting leave the plaintiff’s loss as damnum absque injuria, and that it is not ordinarily a tort to hire the employees of another for use in the hirer’s business. It then states the limit that has carried forward into the modern cases: the immunity against liability is not retained if unfair methods are used in interfering in such advantageous relations. On the facts, the court found the defendant had gained an unfair advantage through deceptive dealings and had intentionally used his own breach of the distribution contract as the means of depriving the plaintiff of his employees, and it was that use of the breach, rather than the hiring itself, that made the conduct tortious. Reeves treated Buxbom as the California precedent closest to an employer’s claim for interference with its own at-will employment relations.

THE COMPETITION RULE REEVES DREW FROM THE COURT OF APPEAL CASES
Reeves surveyed the Court of Appeal authority that had applied the privilege of competition to employment relations, and reproduced the formulation from Diodes, Inc. v. Franzen (1968) 260 Cal.App.2d 244, 255: no actionable wrong is committed by a competitor who solicits or hires away a competitor’s employees who are not under contract, so long as the inducement to leave is not accompanied by unlawful action; but if either the departing employee or the competitor uses unfair or deceptive means to effectuate new employment, or either is guilty of some concomitant, unconscionable conduct, the former employer has a cause of action for the detriment suffered. Reeves also reproduced the Diodes statement that the interests of the employee in his own mobility and betterment are deemed paramount to the competitive business interests of the employers where neither the employee nor the new employer has committed any illegal act accompanying the employment change, and noted the parallel holding in Metro Traffic Control, Inc. v. Shadow Traffic Network (1994) 22 Cal.App.4th 853, 860. The Reeves court observed that, strictly speaking, none of those cases had been brought as interference-with-at-will-employment claims — Diodes was a breach of fiduciary duty case, Metro concerned injunctive relief on noncompete and trade secret theories, and Buxbom was a contract damages case — but concluded that the same considerations support similar limitations in the interference action.

WHETHER AN EMPLOYER MAY SUE AT ALL: REEVES’S DISAPPROVAL OF GAB BUSINESS SERVICES
The defendants in Reeves argued, relying on GAB Business Services, Inc. v. Lindsey & Newsom Claim Services, Inc. (2000) 83 Cal.App.4th 409, that California law does not and should not recognize a cause of action by one employer against another for interference with the contractual relations of at-will employees. GAB had reasoned that expanding the tort to employer claims would invite innumerable lawsuits, undermine the state’s policy supporting employee mobility and betterment, and chill employment opportunities, and that the tort of unfair competition could adequately address unlawful conduct among competing employers. The Reeves court rejected that reasoning on three grounds: that intentionally interfering with an at-will contractual relation is firmly established as actionable in California and no basis appeared for restricting the tort to employees; that neither GAB nor the defendants offered empirical or evidentiary support for the predicted flood of litigation or chilling effect; and that case law in analogous contexts already shields employers who hire a competitor’s at-will employees without engaging in unlawful conduct. The court disapproved GAB to the extent it conflicts with the views expressed in Reeves.
